narrative:

Your class ranking after the third year of law school was the strongest influence, pushing the prediction strongly toward failure. You placed in the bottom decile (1 out of 10) among your classmates, far below the average of roughly the middle of the class for students who were accepted. This low ranking signaled to the model a high risk of struggling with the bar exam.

Your LSAT score was the second most important factor and also increased the likelihood of failure. At 23.5, it sits well below the average of 37.2 among accepted students, indicating weaker preparation in the skills the bar exam tests.

Your undergraduate GPA worked mildly in the opposite direction, slightly lowering the predicted risk of failure. At 2.6 it is below the 3.23 average of accepted students, but the model still saw it as a small positive relative to the other signals.

Taken together, these academic performance indicators created a clear picture of elevated risk. To improve your chances, you should focus on strengthening your study habits and academic performance, consider retaking the LSAT to raise your score, and explore additional bar exam preparation resources before reapplying.
